title: One bad partner message holds up every incoming partner message for every company on the install
description: pullMessages only sets a message aside straight away when it throws PartnerDataError. Any other error (a database rejection, a Prisma error) leaves the cursor just before that message and throws. That stops the whole pull for the install, across all links and all shops, and the message is retried for 3 syncs before it is skipped. The validators let through values the database refuses. For example, dateOf (line 68) accepts any JS-valid date such as "-100000-01-01T00:00:00Z", and Postgres rejects it with error 22009. A hostile partner with a link to any one company on a hosted multi-shop install can therefore keep inbound partner traffic stalled for every company there. Each poisoned message costs about 2 sync intervals, and the hub allows 3000 messages per hour. Side effects: hubState.partnerError (install-wide) is shown on every company's Partners page and carries the Prisma error text, including the source path and values. The 'N messages couldn't be sent' count at line 605 is install-wide, so a company can see a count while its own list is empty.
failure_scenario: The partner (retail side) posts settle.paid with at="-100000-01-01T00:00:00Z", followed by an ordinary job.new. Sync 1 throws and the cursor stays before the poisoned message. Sync 2 does the same. Only sync 3 marks it skipped and applies the job.new. Every other message for every shop on the install waits behind it. Repeating one poisoned message about every 2 minutes stalls intake indefinitely.
suggested_fix: Bound dates in dateOf (for example 2000-01-01 to now+1 year) and throw PartnerDataError otherwise. Run applyMessage plus partnerSeen.create in one transaction. On any non-transient error (Prisma known-request or validation errors), park the message as a failure and continue, rather than stopping the install-wide pull; hold back at most that link. Keep partnerError and the stuck count per shop, and show a generic message instead of raw Prisma text.
evidence:
Own hub (:6581) and own bench DB, driving the real syncPartners() through tsx. Output:
[after sync 1] cursor=1 partnerError="partner message settle.paid from retail: Invalid `db.settlement.create()` invocation ... Database error. Code: `22009`. Message: `time zone displacement out of range: "-100000-01-01 00:00:00"`" legit job.new applied: false; failures tries=1 skipped=false
[after sync 2] cursor=1 ... legit job.new applied: false; tries=2
after sync 3: partnerCursor=3, PartnerFailure settle.paid tries=3 skipped=t, RepairJob legit-job-1 created.
Code: `const skip = e instanceof PartnerDataError || tries >= 3; ... else { await db.hubState.update({ ... partnerCursor: doneThrough }); throw ... }`
verifier_notes: confirmed: Reproduced end to end, with a worse effect than reported: one company's hostile partner held up a different company's inbound messages. dateOf (partners.ts:68) accepts any JS-valid date. Postgres refuses year -100000 with 22009, which is not a PartnerDataError. pullMessages (550-563) then sets the install-wide partnerCursor to just before the message and throws, and the next two syncs do the same before tries >= 3 sets it aside. Each poisoned message therefore costs 2 syncs, about 2 minutes at the default PARTNER_SYNC_SECONDS=60. The hub allows 3000 posts per hour, so a burst of queued poison messages stalls intake for hours. No victim cooperation is needed. Any tenant on a hosted install that is on the hub can make a partner code (makePartnerCode only needs requireAdmin of their own shop) and redeem it through /v1/partners/join, which needs no join key. That tenant then controls the partner side of a link to their own shop and can stall partner intake for every company on the install. Side effects also hold: hubState.partnerError is install-wide, holds the raw Prisma text (source path and code excerpt), and is shown on every company's Partners page (partners/page.tsx:54). The stuck count at line 605 has no shopId filter. Round 1 (8b3e5f2) added this quarantine to stop one bad message holding up the rest, so this is an incomplete fix. The NUL-byte variant is not a vector: the hub's jsonb refuses it with a 500. Severity: DoS that needs a partner link, but it crosses tenants on the hosted app, so medium.

title: settle.paid from a partner is booked with no confirmation, no cap and no sign check, so the victim's books show it owes up to $100,000
description: By design, the shop that pays records a settlement and the other shop just applies it. applyMessage accepts netCents anywhere in ±10,000,000 from either side. It does not check that the sign matches the sender (retail should be > 0, repair < 0), does not cap the amount at the running balance, and has no step where the receiver confirms the payment arrived. The balance on /partners/[id] then flips to 'You owe <partner> $100,000.00', and the settlement form on the statement page is pre-filled with that amount (statement/page.tsx: defaultValue when balance < 0 on the repair side). consign.return works the same way: the sewing shop's claim moves stock back onto the repair shop's shelf and is capped only at the on-shelf count.
failure_scenario: A hostile sewing shop sends settle.paid {netCents: 10000000, note: 'paid in full'} without paying. The repair shop's balance goes from 0 to -10,000,000, meaning 'You owe Evil Sewing $100,000.00', and the Record payment form proposes paying it.
suggested_fix: Require the sign to match m.fromSide. Store incoming settlements as 'claimed' and leave them out of the running balance until an admin of the receiving shop confirms receipt, or at least cap an unconfirmed claim at what the sender owed. Show claimed payments separately. Do the same for consign.return (pending until the owner confirms the stock is back).
evidence:
PoC against own hub and DB:
repair shop balance before: 0
hub accepted settle.paid 200
sync: { sent: 0, received: 1 }
repair shop balance after: -10000000 (negative = the repair shop owes the sewing shop)
settlements: [ { netCents: 10000000, byName: 'Evil', note: 'paid in full' } ]
verifier_notes: confirmed: Reproduced. settle.paid (partners.ts:1006-1023) books any netCents in ±10,000,000 from either side. There is no sign check against fromSide, no cap at the balance, and no confirmation step. runningBalance subtracts it at once. The statement page (statement/page.tsx:157-179) then shows '<repair> owes <sewing shop>' and pre-fills the Record payment amount. A partner saying it paid is the design ('The shop that pays records it'). But the file header promises that hostile partners' values are checked for sense, and a claim of $100,000 against a $0 balance, or a wrong-sign amount, is stored without question. The realistic abuse is quieter: a dishonest sewing shop 'settles' exactly what it owes without paying, and the repair shop's books show nothing owed. The victim must first have linked with that partner, and the entry is attributed to the partner by name, so medium rather than high.

title: Buyer's copy of a partner order is never reconciled with the seller's rebuilt lines and prices, so the two statements disagree
description: placePartnerOrder (partner-orders.ts:33) prices the buyer's copy from its local catalog copy. On receipt, order.new rebuilds each line from the seller's current Part (current wholesale price, items no longer offered left out) and only adds a note. order.update messages (partner-orders.ts:156-163) carry status, carrier, tracking and notes, never lines or total. The buyer's PartnerOrder.lines and totalCents therefore stay as ordered. The buyer's statement and running balance use its totalCents. 'Receive' (partner-orders.ts:108-140) adds the buyer's lines to inventory, including items the seller left out. pushCatalogs only re-sends a changed catalog after 10 minutes (line 451), so after any price change or un-offer the buyer orders from a stale catalog for at least that long.
failure_scenario: The repair shop raises the partner price of item X from $14 to $16, or un-offers item Y. Within the catalog window, the sewing shop orders 2 X and 1 Y. Seller copy: 2 x $16 = $32 (Y left out). Buyer copy: 2 x $14 + Y. After delivery and receipt, the buyer's statement and balance show a different amount from the seller's, and the buyer's inventory gains a Y that was never delivered. Neither side is told the totals differ.
suggested_fix: Have the seller send its rebuilt lines and totalCents back: in an 'order.accepted' or on the first order.update, or in DELIVERED, which is what counts on the statement. Have the buyer replace its lines and total with them before DELIVERED or RECEIVED is applied, and receive only what the seller delivered. Also send a changed catalog price immediately, rather than throttling price changes along with stock counts.
evidence: partners.ts:878-889 rebuilds lines: `lines.push({ itemKey: part.id, ..., unitCents: part.wholesaleCents! })`, `notes.push("Left out: ...")`. partner-orders.ts:156-163 sends order.update with `{ id, status, ...extra, sellerNote, eventNote, at }` only. The order.update apply (partners.ts:926-937) updates status, notes and dates only. statementFor uses `o.totalCents` of each shop's own copy (line 1251).
verifier_notes: confirmed: Reproduced with the real sync and apply code. The two server actions need a session, so their DB writes and outgoing messages were copied line for line into the script. On order.new the seller rebuilds lines at the current wholesale price and leaves out items no longer offered (878-889); the differences are recorded only in the seller's own note. order.update carries status and shipping fields, never lines or total (partner-orders.ts:156-163, partners.ts:926-937). The buyer's copy is never corrected. statementFor and runningBalance each use their own copy's totalCents, so the two shops' statements disagree. 'Receive' on the buyer side adds every line of the buyer's copy to inventory, including the item that was left out. pushCatalogs throttles a changed catalog to one send per 10 minutes (line 451), and in the test the second sync did not send the new price. This is a money-consistency bug in a less common flow: a price change or un-offer shortly before an order.
also_reported_as: code: src/lib/partners.ts:877 Partner orders diverge between the two shops when the catalog is stale: the seller re-prices or drops lines and never tells the buyer, so totals, statements and the buyer's inventory disagree

title: Replacing a terms proposal reuses its version number, so an accept of the old proposal splits the two shops' terms permanently (one shows 'both accepted' with withdrawn terms); accept also binds to whatever proposal is in the DB, not what was shown
description: proposeTerms always uses version = termsVersion + 1 (line 305), so 'Proposing again replaces it' (agreement page) reuses the same number. Suppose the partner accepts the first proposal while the replacement is in flight. acceptTerms (line 325-330) adopts it locally as the new version and records the proposer as having accepted too. The proposer's terms.accept handler sees the key mismatch and sets the accept aside (line 718, PartnerDataError). The accepter's terms.propose handler then ignores the replacement because version <= termsVersion (line 700). The error text says 'propose them again', but every re-proposal is again termsVersion+1 = 2 and is ignored the same way. The two sides now run on different terms. The sewing shop recomputes repair commission from its own copy (job.update, line 772) and its consignment share at the register, while the repair shop uses its copy, so the statements disagree. Separately, AcceptForm (agreement/page.tsx:92) posts only name and agree. acceptTerms reads l.proposedTerms fresh (line 321), so if a newer proposal arrived after the page loaded, the click accepts terms the user never saw.
failure_scenario: The repair shop proposes a 20% commission (v2). The sewing shop, with v2 on screen, accepts, while the repair shop replaces its proposal with 25% before the next sync. Result: the sewing shop is at v2, 20%, and shows 'Both shops accepted version 2'. The repair shop is at v1, 15%, still 'waiting'. Proposing again changes nothing. From then on the sewing shop credits itself 20% commission and the repair shop 15%.
suggested_fix: Never reuse a proposal number: version = max(termsVersion, proposedTerms?.version ?? 0) + 1. Make the proposer's confirmation authoritative. On an accept whose key doesn't match, the proposer should answer (for example, re-send its current proposal with a higher version, or send 'terms.reject'), and the accepter should reopen instead of staying 'agreed'. The accepter should not record the proposer's acceptance until that confirmation arrives. In terms.propose, don't silently ignore version <= termsVersion when the key differs from the current terms; treat it as a conflict to show. Put the displayed version and termsKey in hidden inputs on AcceptForm, and have acceptTerms refuse if the stored proposal no longer matches.
evidence:
Reproduced on the isolated instance (two Playwright pages; the accept and the re-proposal were clicked together so they went out in the same kicked sync):
after proposal X (20%): repair | v1 | 15 | proposed 2 @20% by repair ; retail | v1 | 15 | proposed 2 @20% by repair
after race: repair | v1 | commission 15 | accepted {} | proposed 2 @25% by repair
            retail | v2 | commission 20 | accepted {"repair": {... "version": 2}, "retail": {"name": "Pat Quilter", "version": 2}} | proposed -
set-aside incoming (repair): terms.accept: the partner accepted different terms from the ones offered; propose them again
sewing shop page says both accepted: 1
after the repair shop proposes again: (unchanged on both sides)
verifier_notes: confirmed: proposeTerms always uses version = termsVersion + 1 (partners.ts:305), so replacing a pending proposal reuses the same number (the agreement page says 'Proposing again replaces it'). If the sewing shop accepts the first v2 before it pulls the replacement, acceptTerms adopts it: termsVersion 2, both marked accepted (325-330). The repair shop's terms.accept handler sees a key mismatch and sets the accept aside (718). The sewing shop's terms.propose handler then ignores the replacement, and every later repair proposal, because `version <= link.termsVersion` (700), and each repair re-proposal is again v2 since the repair shop's termsVersion is still 1. The only way out is for the sewing shop to propose v3, and it has no reason to, because its page shows both shops accepted. Commission is computed from each side's own terms (job.update at 772 on the sewing side; jobSnapshot on the repair side), so the statements disagree. The second part also holds: AcceptForm posts only name and agree (agreement/page.tsx:92-102), and acceptTerms reads l.proposedTerms fresh (321). A same-number replacement that arrives after the page loads overwrites proposedTerms (the guard at 703 only skips when this shop is the repair-side proposer), so the click accepts terms the user never saw. The race needs the accept to fall inside roughly a 60 s sync window or an offline period, which makes it a less common flow, hence medium.
also_reported_as: security: src/lib/partners.ts:317 Accepting partner terms isn't tied to the terms the person read

title: Install-level hub refusals (401/403) dead-letter each partner message one by one, and later messages go out ahead of them
description: pushOutbox treats any 4xx other than 408/429 as 'refused for good' for that message: it sets deadAt and does not hold back the partnership. A 401 (hub restored or moved without this install) or a 403 (install blocked, then unblocked) is not about the message. While it lasts, every waiting and newly created message is dead-lettered. Afterwards each must be re-sent by hand ('Send again', 30 shown at a time), in whatever order the user clicks, after later messages have already gone. For example, job.paid can go out before its job.new, and the receiver silently drops messages for jobs it doesn't know.
failure_scenario: The hub admin blocks the install for an hour, and meanwhile the sewing shop takes in three machines and rings up a payment. All four messages are marked dead. After the unblock nothing is sent until someone re-sends each one, and a job.paid re-sent before its job.new is lost on the repair side.
suggested_fix: Treat 401 and 403 (and 404 'No such partner link') as install-level or link-level conditions: stop the push, keep the messages waiting (not dead), and show the cause. Reserve deadAt for message-specific refusals (400, 413). When a dead message is re-sent, keep holding later messages of the same link until it is sent.
evidence: `const forGood = status >= 400 && status < 500 && status !== 408 && status !== 429; ... ...(forGood ? { deadAt: new Date() } : { nextTryAt: ... }); if (!forGood) held.add(key);`
verifier_notes: confirmed: The code does what the finding says. Sync order is pushJobUpdates → pushCatalogs → pushOutbox, and the first two never call the hub, so pushOutbox is the first thing to reach it. A blocked install gets 403 on every /v1 route from the hub's member middleware (server.mjs:153), and an unknown install gets 401 (server.mjs:152). hubFetch throws HubError(status), and hubStatus returns 403 or 401. pushOutbox treats `forGood` (4xx except 408/429) as final and sets deadAt without holding the link. Up to 300 waiting messages per sync, across every company and link on the install, are dead-lettered one by one, and so is every new message on later syncs while the block lasts. Nothing re-queues them after the unblock: resendPartnerMessage clears deadAt for one message at a time (admin only, 30 shown per company). Round 1 (8b3e5f2) added the forGood rule and round 2 (9ba25a4) fixed the held-key ordering, but neither separates install-level 401/403 from message-level refusals. Correction to the example: job.paid overtaking its own job.new can't happen in the normal flow, because the register only offers jobs that are READY and carry totalCents, which means the repair shop already has the job. Pairs that really can be reordered by clicking 'Send again' out of order: job.new/job.cancel (the cancel is dropped by repairSideJob → null, then the job is created), order.new/order.update CANCELLED (the update is dropped because `!o`), and consign.sale/its -void (the void is set aside as bad data, then the sale counts). The page lists messages oldest first, so reordering needs the user to click out of order. The main impact is that all partner traffic on the install stops until every message is re-sent by hand. The trigger (a hub block, or a lost/restored hub) is rare, so medium.

title: Voiding a consigned sale leaves the two partners' consignment balances out of step (rounding and terms changes)
description: voidSale (register.ts:349-351) records the void's shopKeepsCents as exactly the negative of the original sale's. The repair shop's consign.sale handler validates the '-void' id against the original but then recomputes shopKeepsCents as Math.round(gross * terms.consignSharePct / 100) from today's terms. Math.round rounds -x.5 toward +infinity, so any sale whose share lands on a half cent comes out 1 cent different after a void (e.g. a $10.05 item at 30%). If the consignment share was changed between the sale and the void, the difference is the whole share delta. Statements and runningBalance on each side sum these rows, so the partners' 'owed' totals disagree and settlements will not net to zero.
failure_scenario: The sewing shop sells a consigned $10.05 item (share 30%): both sides record shopKeeps 302. The owner voids it. The sewing shop records -302; the repair shop records Math.round(-301.5) = -301. Sewing shop net owed for sale+void is 0; repair shop's is -1. If the terms moved to 40% before the void, the repair shop's net becomes +$1.00 for a sale that no longer exists.
suggested_fix: In the consign.sale handler, when the id ends with '-void' and `original` is found, store `shopKeepsCents: original.shopKeepsCents != null ? -original.shopKeepsCents : -Math.round((Math.round(original.qty*original.priceCents) * terms.consignSharePct)/100)`. Better still, put one shared share helper (round half away from zero) in partner-terms.ts and use it on both sides.
evidence: register.ts:351 `shopKeepsCents: original?.shopKeepsCents != null ? -original.shopKeepsCents : null`; partners.ts:971-987 loads `original` for '-void' ids but stores `shopKeepsCents: Math.round((gross * terms.consignSharePct) / 100)`. A tsx model of both formulas printed: { holderSaleKeeps: 302, holderVoidKeeps: -302, ownerSaleKeeps: 302, ownerVoidKeeps: -301 } / 'holder net owed after sale+void: 0' / 'owner net owed after sale+void: -1' / 'owner after terms change: 100'.
verifier_notes: confirmed: voidSale (register.ts:349-351) stores the void's shopKeepsCents as exactly -original.shopKeepsCents. The repair shop's consign.sale handler (partners.ts:969-987, reworked in 9ba25a4) looks up `original` for '-void' ids only to validate it, then recomputes shopKeepsCents as Math.round(gross * terms.consignSharePct / 100) with today's terms (terms = normalizeTerms(link.terms) at line 695). Math.round(-x.5) rounds toward +infinity, so any consigned price whose share lands on a half cent disagrees by 1 cent after a void. At 30% that is any gross ending in 5 cents, e.g. $12.95 gives 389 vs -388, and prices ending in .95 are common. If the share was renegotiated between the sale and the void, the two sides differ by the whole share delta. Both sides' runningBalance and statementFor sum consignShare(), which uses the stored shopKeepsCents, so the two books' balances diverge.

code: src/lib/partners.ts:987 Voided consigned sale: the repair shop recomputes the sewing shop's share (current terms, Math.round of a negative) instead of negating the original, so the two statements stop agreeing

title: job.paid marks the job paid and freezes its commission even when the sewing shop collected less than the repair shop's current bill; the remainder can never be collected through the partner flow
description: The sewing shop's register charges repairDue() from its local copy of totalCents (register.ts:66,186) and sets paidAt. On the repair shop, job.paid sets paidAt: job.paidAt ?? at whatever the amount (line 828), which fixes paidAt and the commission in jobSnapshot. If the repair shop added a line after the sewing shop's last job.update, the later update raises totalCents on the sewing side, but the job keeps paidAt. pickupJobs filters paidAt: null and completeSale rejects paid jobs, so the balance can't be rung up. Each side also froze commission from a different bill.
failure_scenario: The repair shop adds a $30 service line to a READY machine at 10:00. At 10:00:30, before the sewing shop's next sync, the customer pays the old $120 at the sewing shop's counter. The repair ticket shows $30 still due, the job is 'paid' on both sides, and the commission differs (15% of $120 vs 15% of $150).
suggested_fix: On the repair side, set paidAt only when SHOP_COLLECTED plus direct payments cover the current total. Send the current due in the next job.update; on the sewing side, a due greater than 0 clears paidAt or lists the remainder in pickupJobs. Alternatively, have job.paid carry the totalCents it paid against, and have the repair shop answer with the difference.
evidence: partners.ts:821-829 (no comparison of amount against the repair shop's total); register.ts:96-99 pickupJobs where paidAt: null; register.ts:168 'if (j.paidAt) throw new UserError(`Repair tag ${j.tag} is already paid.`)'
verifier_notes: confirmed: Traced end to end. The sewing shop's register charges repairDue() from its local copy (register.ts:66,186) and sets paidAt; completeSale rejects jobs already paid (register.ts:170), and pickupJobs lists only paidAt null (register.ts:97). The repair shop's job.paid handler (partners.ts:821-829) records a SHOP_COLLECTED payment for whatever amount arrives and sets paidAt = job.paidAt ?? at without comparing it to the ticket total. From then on jobSnapshot keeps the commission it already had (line 372). The repair shop's commissionCents was last written by pushJobUpdates after the extra line (a ticket edit calls kickPartnerSync, tickets.ts:23), so it reflects the higher bill. The sewing shop froze its commission when it marked the job paid, from its older lines (partners.ts:772), and its later job.update never clears paidAt (line 786). Result: both sides show the job paid; the repair ticket still has a balance that the partner register can't collect; the two statements (jobOwed = paidCents - commissionCents) differ by commission% × the added amount. The race window is the sewing install's sync lag: 60 s by default (PARTNER_SYNC_SECONDS). Round 2's offline mode lets the register keep selling from the stale local copy while the hub is unreachable, so the window can be much longer. The flow is less common, but it produces wrong money totals between the shops, hence medium. Minor: the reviewer cited register.ts:168; the check is at line 170.

title: Hub quotas are per install, so on a hosted multi-company install one company can use up partner codes and messages for all
description: All companies on a hosted StitchBench share one hub install key. The hub limits invites (30/h), redeems (20/h) and partner messages (3000/h) per install (stitchhub partners.mjs:111,134,172). The bench has no per-company quota: makePartnerCode, enterPartnerCode and any action that queues a message (countConsigned and returnConsigned only need requireUser) can be repeated freely. One company's admin, or even a TECH user, can exhaust the budget. Every other company's partner messages then get 429 and back off for up to 30 minutes, and their partner codes fail.
failure_scenario: A user of company A submits the shelf count form about once a second for an hour. The install's 3000 messages per hour are used up, and company B's job.paid and job.new messages are delayed (429, exponential back-off).
suggested_fix: Add per-company rate limits on the bench for code creation, redemption and message-producing actions. Have the hub key its limits by (install, shopRef) as well as by install.
evidence: hub: `allow(`pmsg:${c.get("install").id}`, 3000)`, `allow(`pinvite:${...install.id}`, 30)`, `allow(`predeem:${...}`, 20)`. Bench: sendToPartner and createPartnerInvite have no per-shop limit.
verifier_notes: confirmed: The bench keeps one hub identity for the whole install: the HubState row id=1 holds the install key, and hubFetch always sends it. The hub's partner limits are in-memory fixed one-hour buckets keyed only by install id (partners.mjs:111 pinvite 30/h, :134 predeem 20/h, checked before the code is validated so bad tries count too, :172 pmsg 3000/h). On the bench, makePartnerCode and enterPartnerCode need only requireAdmin, which any company owner has, including anyone who signs up when ALLOW_SIGNUP=true and SETUP_TOKEN is unset. countConsigned, returnConsigned and syncPartnersNow need only requireUser. None of them has a per-company limit. One tenant can therefore use up the install's invite or redeem quota for an hour, again and again: 30 'make code' clicks or 20 bad codes. With a partner link it can also flood messages, and every other company's partner messages then get 429 and exponential back-off (not lost, only delayed). This is a cross-tenant DoS that needs a sign-in, so medium. The reviewer's low rating understates it on the hosted multi-company deployment.

title: placeConsignment stores negative shelf prices and unbounded/over-stock quantities, corrupting the repair shop's own inventory and permanently diverging from the partner
description: The repair-shop consignment action validates far more weakly than the message applier that consumes it. qty (line 181-183) is only checked for `qty > 0` with no upper bound and no check against qtyOnHand, and price (line 184-185) is only rejected when falsy (0/null) — a negative shelf price passes `if (!price)`. So the repair shop can place a negative-priced consignment, or a quantity larger than its stock or larger than the partner will accept. The item is written to ConsignItem (with the bad price/qty) and the repair shop's Part.qtyOnHand is decremented unconditionally (line 188), driving it negative. The corresponding consign.place hub message is then rejected on the sewing-shop side, because receiveConsigned uses `int(it.priceCents, 0, MAX_MONEY)` and `qtyOf` (|qty| <= MAX_QTY=100000) in src/lib/partners.ts — so the placement silently half-completes: recorded on the repair side, quarantined on the sewing side, and shown as if the *partner* sent bad data.
failure_scenario: Repair shop opens Partners > (partner) > Consignment, picks a part with 10 on hand, enters qty 3 and shelf price -9.00 -> 'Placed on their shelf'. DB: Part.qtyOnHand 10->7, ConsignItem placed=3 priceCents=-900, outbox consign.place priceCents=-900. On the next sync the sewing shop sets the message aside ('shelf price is out of range') so the item never appears on their shelf, and it lands under 'Messages that didn't get through'. Entering qty 1000000 similarly succeeds locally (stock -> negative, e.g. -999982) and is quarantined ('qty is out of range').
suggested_fix: Validate before placing: reject price <= 0 or > MAX_MONEY (e.g. `if (!(price > 0) || price > 10_000_000) throw UserError`), cap/round qty to the same MAX_QTY the applier enforces, and reject qty greater than part.qtyOnHand (or explicitly allow negative stock, but then the applier must accept the same values). Mirror the limits in src/lib/partners.ts so both sides agree.
evidence: Ran step9-negprice.js against the live app (shops QA Repair R / QA Sewing S on the shared install): before: '10 @900'; neg-price place toast 'Placed on their shelf'; after part '7 @900'; consignItem '3 placed @-900'; outbox consign.place priceCents '-900'. step8 with qty=1e6 produced Part.qtyOnHand=-999982 and sewing-shop PartnerFailure rows 'consign.place: shelf price is out of range' and 'consign.place: qty is out of range' (visible on the Partners page). Code: `const raw = Number(str(formData.get("qty")) ?? "0"); const qty = ... Math.round(raw); if (!(qty > 0)) throw...; const price = toCents(formData.get("price")) ?? part.priceCents; if (!price) throw...` — no negative/upper-bound/stock guard, then `qtyOnHand: { decrement: qty }`.
verifier_notes: confirmed: The code is described correctly. placeConsignment (src/actions/partner-orders.ts:181-185) checks only `qty > 0` and `if (!price)`. toCents('-9.00') returns -900, so a negative price passes, and nothing caps qty at the applier's MAX_QTY. The receiving side's receiveConsigned (src/lib/partners.ts:1129-1133) uses int(priceCents, 0, MAX_MONEY) and qtyOf (|x| <= 100000), so the sewing shop sets the message aside as a PartnerDataError. The repair shop has already written the ConsignItem and cut its stock, and it is told 'Placed on their shelf'. Nothing on the repair side reports the refusal: the failure appears only on the partner's Partners page. The repair shop also can't undo the placement, because returnConsigned and countConsigned are sewing-side only. One part of the claim is overstated: placing more than qtyOnHand (stock going negative) matches the rest of the app, which decrements stock unguarded in register.ts:257, tickets.ts:303 and scan.ts:68. The real defect is values outside the partner's accepted range. I found an extra consequence: a huge qty drives the repair shop's stock below -100000. After that every catalog message is set aside with 'stock is out of range', so the partner's catalog stops updating.
also_reported_as: security: src/actions/partner-orders.ts:185 placeConsignment checks less than the receiving shop, so bad input leaves one-sided consignment records

title: partnerOrderAction checks the order status outside the transaction and updates without a status condition: two concurrent Delivered or Received clicks move stock twice
description: The order is read before the transaction (line 79). The status checks (lines 89-104, 111) use that stale copy, and tx.partnerOrder.update (line 146) has no status in its where clause. Two submits of 'Delivered' from two tabs or two staff both pass, both decrement stock for every line (line 101), and both queue an order.update. The same applies to 'Received' on the buyer side (stock added twice). Mixed actions misbehave too. Accept and Deliver clicked together can leave the order ACCEPTED after its stock was taken, so it can be delivered, and decremented, again. Cancel and Deliver together can leave it CANCELLED with the stock gone.
failure_scenario: The repair shop has the order open in two tabs, or two employees work the order queue, and both press 'Delivered' on an order of 4. Stock drops by 8, two SOLD stock moves are written, and the sewing shop gets two DELIVERED updates.
suggested_fix: Inside the transaction, first claim the transition. Run tx.partnerOrder.updateMany({ where: { shopId, id: o.id, status: { in: allowedFrom } }, data: { status: next, ... } }) and throw a UserError if the count is 0. Only then move stock and queue the message. Alternatively, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the order row in the transaction and re-check its status.
evidence:
Reproduced on the isolated instance with two pages clicking 'Delivered' at once:
repair shop stock of QA-P1: before 18, after delivering an order of 4: 10
stock moves: ... / -4 PO-1002 to QA Quilt Corner / -4 PO-1002 to QA Quilt Corner
order.update messages queued: 2
verifier_notes: confirmed: partnerOrderAction reads the order before the transaction (partner-orders.ts:79) and checks the state transition against that copy (89-110). The final tx.partnerOrder.update has no status in its where clause (146-147), and there is no row lock. Under Postgres READ COMMITTED, two concurrent 'Delivered' submits both pass the check. Both run the atomic `qtyOnHand: { decrement: l.qty }` for every line (101), write two SOLD stock moves and queue two order.update messages. The same applies to two 'Received' submits on the buyer side, which add stock twice. Accept and Deliver interleaved can end ACCEPTED after stock was taken, so the order can be delivered, and stock taken, again. The UI does not prevent this across tabs or users: the Accept and Delivered forms are both shown on PLACED orders (orders/[orderId]/page.tsx). Within one tab the router's action queue serializes the actions, and a stale tab re-reads status, so it takes two genuinely concurrent requests. The window is narrow, but the result is corrupted stock counts, and voidSale in the same codebase already uses the correct updateMany-with-status pattern.
also_reported_as: code: src/actions/partner-orders.ts:93 Partner status transitions check a stale row: two concurrent 'Delivered' (or 'Received') clicks both move stock
qa: src/actions/partner-orders.ts:92 Partner order 'Delivered' is not guarded against concurrent submits, double-decrementing the seller's stock

title: Messages the sender accepts but the receiver rejects are silently lost: e.g. a machine intake with a negative pre-approved amount never reaches the repair shop, and the sewing shop is never told
description: The sender validates less than the receiver's apply code. takeInMachine stores preApprovedCents = toCents(formData.get('preApproved')) without a range check (the intake field is a free-text inputMode=decimal). newJobFromPartner requires optInt(d.preApprovedCents, 0, MAX_MONEY) (partners.ts:1075/1099), throws PartnerDataError, and pullMessages sets the message aside immediately (partners.ts:550). The same happens with placeConsignment: toCents can be negative ('if (!price)' only rejects 0; partner-orders.ts:184-185), and receiveConsigned requires int(0..MAX_MONEY) (partners.ts:1133). Messages dropped as NEW_WORK after a link ends (partners.ts:692) also vanish without a trace. The sender has already committed local state (a tagged job, or stock taken off its shelf) and its outbox row is marked sent. The only trace is a 'set aside' line on the receiver's Partners page. Every later message about the same record (job.cancel, job.paid, consign.sale...) is then applied against missing state and silently ignored (e.g. 'if (!job?.ticketId) return').
failure_scenario: The sewing shop takes a machine in and a clerk types '-20' as the pre-approved amount. The customer gets a claim tag and the machine goes on the shelf for pickup, but the repair shop never gets a ticket. The sewing shop's job stays 'Here, waiting for the repair shop' indefinitely and nobody on the sewing side is warned.
suggested_fix: Share one validator module between the sending actions and applyMessage, and reject bad input at the sender: preApproved 0..MAX_MONEY, a consignment price > 0 and <= MAX_MONEY, qty bounds, and so on. Also make rejection visible to the sender: when the receiver sets a message aside or drops it as NEW_WORK, queue a 'msg.rejected' reply {type, id, reason}. The sender should flag the local record (job, order, consignment) and list it under 'Messages that didn't get through'.
evidence:
Reproduced on the isolated instance through /repairs/new:
sewing shop job rows: retail AT_SHOP_AWAITING_PICKUP preApproved=-2000
sewing shop outbox job.new: sent=true dead=false
repair shop set-aside: job.new skipped=true: pre-approved is out of range
sewing shop Partners page shows a problem: 0
(no RepairJob or Ticket row on the repair shop)
verifier_notes: confirmed: takeInMachine stores `preApprovedCents = toCents(formData.get('preApproved'))` with no range check (repair-jobs.ts:84). The field is free text with inputMode=decimal (intake-form.tsx:164), and toCents('-20') returns -2000. The hub does not validate message data (stitchhub partners.mjs:171-187 checks only id, type and size), so the sender's outbox row is marked sent. The receiver's newJobFromPartner calls optInt(d.preApprovedCents, 0, MAX_MONEY), which throws PartnerDataError inside the transaction (partners.ts:1075). pullMessages then sets the message aside at once and marks it seen (550, 560). The only trace is on the receiver's Partners page. The sender's warning counts only dead or retried outbox rows (605), so the sewing shop is never told, and later job.cancel, job.paid and similar messages hit `if (!job?.ticketId) return`. placeConsignment has the same gap: `if (!price)` only rejects 0 (partner-orders.ts:184-185), so a negative shelf price takes stock off the repair shop's shelf and is then rejected by receiveConsigned (int 0..MAX_MONEY, partners.ts:1133). Round 1 added the matching range check to answerEstimate (approvedCents) but not to the intake's preApproved, so that fix was incomplete. It is also a small partial write: the Machine row is created outside the transaction (1059), so a rejected job.new leaves an orphan machine on the repair shop. This is missing validation that stores bad data and silently loses a job, which the rubric rates medium, although it takes an unusual entry to trigger.

title: A second estimate on a partner repair never reaches the sewing shop: 'approval' is never reset, so the answer form and to-do stay hidden
description: The sewing shop's 'needs the customer's OK' form shows only when `j.status === "WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK" && !j.approval`, and the dashboard PartnerTodo filters `approval: null`. The approval is set once by answerEstimate (or job.reply on the repair side) and never cleared. The job.update handler (src/lib/partners.ts:754-789) updates status, lines and totals but not approval or approvedCents. If the repair shop needs the customer's OK again (more damage found after the first approval, or a cheaper offer after a decline) and sets the ticket back to 'Waiting on customer OK', the retail job goes to WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK but still carries the old APPROVED or DECLINED. The sewing shop is never prompted and sees only the stale 'Customer approved up to $X' pill. The repair side's ticket page also keeps showing the old approval pill.
failure_scenario: Round 1: customer approves up to $150. The tech finds a cracked hook, adds $120 of parts and sets 'Waiting on customer OK' again. On the sewing shop, /repairs/<id> shows no approve or decline form, the dashboard to-do doesn't list it, and the job sits in 'Needs the customer's OK' with a pill saying it was already approved. The repair stalls, or the tech goes ahead on the stale approval.
suggested_fix: When a job moves into WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK from another status, clear approval and approvedCents on both sides: in the retail job.update handler when status changes to WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK, and on the repair side in setStatus or pushJobUpdates for the job's RepairJob. Or record the time of the approval and compare it with the time of the latest WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK event, showing the form when the request is newer.
evidence: repairs/[id]/page.tsx:44 `{j.status === "WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK" && !j.approval && (`; partner-todo.tsx:14 `where: { shopId, side: "retail", status: "WAITING_CUSTOMER_OK", approval: null }`; partners.ts job.update data block (lines 770-787) has no approval or approvedCents; `grep approval src/lib/partners.ts` shows it written only by job.reply (812). answerEstimate (repair-jobs.ts:151) itself would accept a second answer; only the UI and to-do hide it.
verifier_notes: confirmed: Nothing ever resets approval. It is written only by answerEstimate (repair-jobs.ts:158) and job.reply (partners.ts:812), and the retail job.update handler (partners.ts:754-790) updates status, lines and totals but not approval or approvedCents. The answer form on /repairs/[id] needs `!j.approval` (page.tsx:44), and PartnerTodo filters `approval: null` (partner-todo.tsx:14). So when the repair shop sets 'Waiting on customer OK' a second time (a re-estimate after an approval, or a new offer after a decline), the sewing shop gets no form and no to-do item and still sees the old approved or declined pill. answerEstimate would accept a second answer, but the UI never offers it. This is a broken flow in a less common but realistic path.
also_reported_as: qa: src/app/(app)/repairs/[id]/page.tsx:44 A second estimate from the repair shop can't be answered: the sewing shop's job page hides the approve/decline form once any approval exists

title: Partner message feed has no byte cap: a hostile partner permanently wedges a victim's entire partner sync
description: GET /v1/partners/messages (partners.mjs:190-224) builds a JSON response from up to `limit` message rows (default/max 500; the app requests limit=200), but each partner_messages.data may be up to 4 MB (MAX_MESSAGE, enforced only per-message on POST at line 179). The page CTE limits by seq count only (LIMIT $3), and the CROSS JOIN can double the rows. There is no cap on the total serialized size. Once a link accumulates ~130 large messages the whole page exceeds V8's max string length (~512 MB) and `c.json(...)` throws `RangeError: Invalid string length`, returning 500. Because the app's pullMessages (stitchbench src/lib/partners.ts:528) always re-requests from the same `since` cursor and only advances it on success, the 500 is fatal: the victim install can never get past those messages, so its ENTIRE partner sync (every partnership, not just the hostile one — the feed spans all of the install's links) is permanently broken and no repair jobs, orders, consignment or settlements flow. The attacker only needs to be on a link with the victim, which even an invite-only 'partner' scope install can be (server.mjs:155 allows /v1/partners/* for scope=partner), so a non-member can wedge a member.
failure_scenario: Attacker redeems a partner invite from victim V (partner scope, no join key needed). Attacker POSTs ~135 messages of ~4 MB each to the link (all accepted, 200). V's next partner sync calls GET /v1/partners/messages?since=0&limit=200; the hub tries to serialize >512 MB, throws RangeError, returns 500. V's cursor never advances; every subsequent sync fails the same way. V's partner integration is dead until an admin manually deletes rows from the DB.
suggested_fix: Cap the partner-message feed by bytes as well as rows: accumulate serialized size while building the page and stop early (returning `more:true` with a `next` cursor that advances past what was returned), or exclude oversized messages from the JSON list and expose them via a separate per-message fetch (like listing/photo bytes). Ensure the returned `next` always advances so a single large message can never stall the cursor. Same pattern is needed for /v1/orders and /v1/changes (see separate finding).
evidence:
Reproduced on a local hub. lib call sent 135 messages of `"a".repeat(4*1024*1024-100)` as job.new data:
  sent 135 max-size messages
  victim feed before: 200 bytes 530
  victim feed after: 500 {"error":"Something went wrong on the hub."} 4059ms
  victim feed again: 500
Hub log: `RangeError: Invalid string length` at server.mjs:158 (the c.json error path). Code: partners.mjs:171-186 caps a single message body to MAX_MESSAGE (4 MB) but the GET at :190-224 only limits row COUNT (line 193 `Math.min(Math.max(Number(limit)||200,1),500)`) and emits `data: m.data` (line 218) with no aggregate size limit.
verifier_notes:
confirmed: Traced end-to-end. partners.mjs:190-224 builds the feed with `data: m.data` for up to `limit` (max 500, app uses 200) rows; the only size guard is the per-message 4MB cap on POST (line 179) and feedLimit()/LIMIT cap rows by COUNT only (db.mjs feedLimit is a seq high-water for read-consistency, not a byte cap). No aggregate byte cap exists. On the app side, pullMessages (bench src/lib/partners.ts:528-575) reads via hubFetch which throws on !r.ok, so a 500 aborts pullMessages before `since = r.next` runs; doPartnerSync catches, records partnerError and rethrows, leaving partnerCursor unadvanced -> every subsequent sync re-requests the same page and fails identically, wedging the install's ENTIRE partner sync (the feed spans all of that install's links, not just the hostile one) until DB surgery. server.mjs:155 lets scope=partner reach /v1/partners/*, and /v1/partners/join (partners.mjs) issues a partner-scope install from just an invite, so a non-member can wedge a member. Prior round 28842a1 added only per-POST body limits (partner message/invite) and read-consistency feed positions, not a feed byte cap, so it does not mitigate this.
confirmed: Every leg traced end-to-end. partner_messages.data is jsonb (migrations/005_partners.sql:44) so it round-trips to a full JS string; the GET /v1/partners/messages feed (src/partners.mjs:190-224) inlines `data: m.data` (line 218) with NO aggregate byte cap — the only limits are row-count (LIMIT $3) and the row-count `more` (Set(...).size >= limit). MAX_MESSAGE caps a single message at 4 MB (enforced only on POST). In the cross-tenant attacker->victim case the CROSS JOIN yields exactly one row per message, so ~130 messages of ~4 MB (total > V8 MAX_STRING_LENGTH 536,870,888) make c.json's JSON.stringify throw RangeError: Invalid string length, which app.onError (server.mjs:90) turns into 500 {"error":"Something went wrong on the hub."}. On the app side pullMessages/doPartnerSync (stitchbench src/lib/partners.ts:528,594) only writes partnerCursor on success and rethrows on the 500, so the cursor never advances: the victim install's ENTIRE inbound partner sync (the feed spans all of the install's links) is permanently wedged until rows are deleted from the DB (KEEP_DAYS=365). Reachable by a partner-scope (non-member) install: server.mjs:158 allows /v1/partners/* for scope=partner and a partner-scope install can create/redeem invites. Not fixed by prior round 28842a1 (that added holdFeeds/feedLimit ordering safety and per-MESSAGE bodyLimit; neither caps the aggregate RESPONSE). Severity high: persistent, total DoS of a core cross-shop flow (jobs, orders, consignment, settlements) affecting all of the victim's partnerships, needing out-of-band DB surgery to recover.
also_reported_as: security: src/partners.mjs:190 One partner (or ex-partner) can permanently wedge a victim install's partner sync and OOM the shared hub with big messages
code: src/partners.mjs:193 Partner message feed has no byte budget: one partner can permanently wedge a shop's whole partner channel (and push GBs into hub memory)

title: Hub partner channel: any member can store unbounded 4 MB messages (self-link, and new installs minted via /partners/join)
description: The only limits on /partners/links/:id/messages are 4 MB per message and 3000 messages per hour per install. Messages are kept for 365 days. redeem() lets an install link two of its own made-up shopRefs (it only refuses the identical install+shopRef), so no victim is needed. A member can also turn its own invite codes into brand-new partner-scope installs through /partners/join. Each of those has fresh rate buckets and can create its own invites, which multiplies the per-install quota. At roughly 12 GB/hour per install, the hub's Postgres volume can be filled, taking the community hub and every partner channel down.
failure_scenario: A member registers, creates an invite as shopRef 'a', redeems it as shopRef 'b', and posts incompressible 4 MB job.new messages at the rate limit. The partner_messages table grows about 4 MB per request. Additional installs minted via /partners/join each add another 3000/hour.
suggested_fix: Refuse links where repair_install_id = retail_install_id unless the shopRefs belong to one hosted install that has really set up the other company (or require the redeemer to be another install). Add per-install and per-link storage quotas (bytes per day, and outstanding unread bytes). Rate-limit /partners/join per inviting install as well as per IP, and cap the partner-scope installs one inviter can create. Drop messages once both sides' cursors have passed them, instead of keeping them for 365 days.
evidence:
Own hub on :6581:
self-link via redeem: 200 1d45eb6350f44beaa7f91510
new install minted via join: 200 45975265063b48e6bb98d0ad partner
five posts of ~4 MB random base64: 200 200 200 200 200
pg_total_relation_size('partner_messages'): 64 kB -> 21 MB after 5 requests.
verifier_notes: confirmed: Reproduced on my own hub. redeem() refuses a link only when both install and shopRef are the same (partners.mjs:65), so one member can link shopRef 'a' to shopRef 'b'. /v1/partners/join turns the member's own invite into a new partner-scope install. That install passes the member middleware for /v1/partners/* (server.mjs:155), so it can make invites of its own, and each new install gets fresh pmsg:/pinvite: buckets. Each message may be 4 MB (bodyLimit is MAX_MESSAGE + 64 KB) at 3000 per hour per install, and messages are kept 365 days (KEEP_DAYS). There is no per-install or per-link byte quota. Three incompressible 4 MB posts grew partner_messages by about 13 MB, so one install can add about 12 GB/hour to the hub's Postgres. It is a DoS that needs a member key or one invite code. The hub admin can block installs, but each minted install must be blocked separately. Medium.
also_reported_as: code: src/partners.mjs:171 Partner channel has no storage quota, and partner-only installs can spawn more installs without the join key

title: Unauthenticated partner-join (and register) limits are keyed on the client's own X-Forwarded-For, and the buckets map is never pruned
description: /v1/partners/join and /v1/register take the rate-limit key from the first X-Forwarded-For entry, which the client controls: behind a proxy that appends, the first entry is still the one the attacker sent. So the 10-per-hour limit is bypassed by changing the header. Each distinct key adds an entry to the in-memory `buckets` Map (server.mjs:74-85), and entries are never removed, so an unauthenticated client can grow hub memory without limit. Guessing codes stays impractical (about 59 bits), but the limit gives no protection.
failure_scenario: A client sends millions of /v1/partners/join requests with random X-Forwarded-For values. None is throttled, and the buckets Map grows until the hub runs out of memory.
suggested_fix: Use the proxy-appended (right-most trusted) address or the platform's client-IP header, prune expired buckets (e.g. sweep entries older than an hour), and add a global cap for unauthenticated routes.
evidence: `const ip = c.req.header("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0].trim() ?? "local"; if (!allow(`pjoin:${ip}`, 10))`. In testing, /v1/register answered 'Too many tries' for plain requests and succeeded again as soon as a random X-Forwarded-For was added (t6.mjs).
verifier_notes: confirmed: The finding is accurate. The rate-limit key for both /v1/register (server.mjs:124-125) and /v1/partners/join (partners.mjs:142-143) is the first X-Forwarded-For entry. The client controls that entry whether the hub runs directly under Docker (the header is fully client-supplied) or behind Cloudflare Tunnel or a reverse proxy that appends (the attacker's value stays first). `allow()` (server.mjs:74-85) adds a Map entry per key and never deletes one; nothing else touches `buckets`, and the partner sweep only cleans DB rows. I rate it higher than the reviewer because of two concrete impacts. (1) The 10/hour limit is the only brute-force protection on /v1/register, and the join key is admin-chosen with only an 8-character minimum (admin PUT /join-key, server.mjs:513). A human-memorable key, like the ones in .env examples, can be dictionary-attacked without limit to gain hub membership. (2) The key includes the raw header value, which can be up to about 16 KB. So each unauthenticated request can pin kilobytes of hub heap for the life of the process, and a modest request count can exhaust memory on a small Railway or NAS instance. This is an unauthenticated DoS of the shared hub. Prior round 28842a1 only reformatted these lines and did not address this.
also_reported_as: security: src/partners.mjs:142 /v1/partners/join rate limit trusts client X-Forwarded-For (bypass), is shared hub-wide without a proxy, and the bucket map is never pruned

code: src/partners.mjs:142 Hub: the rate limit on the unauthenticated partner-join route is keyed on a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For, so it is bypassable and grows the in-memory bucket map without bound

title: Any member can store about 12 GB/hour in partner messages kept for a year (a self-link needs no second shop)
description: POST /v1/partners/links/:id/messages accepts messages of up to 4 MB, 3000 per install per hour, and messages are kept for 365 days. Any member can make an invite for shopRef 'a' and redeem it themselves for shopRef 'b' (allowed by design for multi-company installs), which gives a private link to fill. 3000 x 4 MB = 12 GB/hour of jsonb per install, and a join key can register more installs. That fills the hub's Postgres disk and takes down the community, and the sweep only removes messages after a year.
failure_scenario: A member creates an invite (shopRef a) and redeems it (shopRef b). Five 4 MB messages are stored in about 0.7 s, so at the 3000/hour limit the member writes about 12 GB/hour.
suggested_fix: Add a byte budget per install per hour/day (e.g. 200 MB/day) in addition to the message count. Drop data a recipient has already fetched, or cap stored bytes per link. Alert the admin summary on unusual volume.
evidence:
Own hub t5_partners.mjs:
self-link: acb41ef2064c42869fa0132b retail
stored 5 x 4MB messages in 719ms (limit 3000/hour, kept 365 days)
Code: `if (!allow(`pmsg:${...}`, 3000)) ...; MAX_MESSAGE = 4*1024*1024; KEEP_DAYS = 365`
verifier_notes: confirmed: Reproduced on my own hub. An install can redeem its own invite under a different shopRef: redeem() only rejects the case where both install and shopRef are the same. The message route (partners.mjs:171-186; the finding cites line 288, but the file has 249 lines) accepts about 4 MB of data per message and up to 3000 messages per install per hour. Nothing removes messages after they are fetched, and the sweep only deletes rows older than 365 days. With random data, TOAST compression saves nothing, so every message costs about 4 MB of disk. 3000 per hour comes to about 12 GB per hour for one install. Only a join key or a partner code is needed (a partner-scope install may use the partner routes), and a new install can be registered with the join key (the register limit can be bypassed, see id 3). This fits the rubric's 'DoS needing auth'. The admin can block the install, but has no way to remove the stored messages.
